exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```vb
Option Strict On

Module Program
    Sub Main()
        Dim total As Integer = 10
        TOTAL += 5
        Dim label As String = "Total: " & Total
        Console.WriteLine(label)
    End Sub
End Module
```

feedback.message: Not yet — `TOTAL` and `total` are the same variable in Visual Basic.

hints: Visual Basic names are not case-sensitive.
exercises.solution: `total`, `TOTAL` and `Total` all name one variable, so `TOTAL += 5` makes it 15, and `&` turns it into text. Output: `Total: 15`.

exercises.prompt:
With `Option Strict Off`, what does this program print?

```vb
Option Strict Off

Module Program
    Sub Main()
        Dim a As Integer = 5 / 2
        Dim b As Integer = 7 / 2
        Console.WriteLine(a + b)
    End Sub
End Module
```

feedback.message: Not yet — the conversion does not truncate; it rounds. Which way does .NET round a value exactly halfway?
Not yet — that is rounding halves upwards. Visual Basic rounds halves to the nearest even number.

hints: `/` always produces a floating-point result: 2.5 and 3.5.
The implicit conversion to `Integer` rounds halfway values to the even neighbour.
exercises.solution: `5 / 2` is 2.5 and `7 / 2` is 3.5. Converting to `Integer` rounds, and halfway values go to the nearest even number: 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4. The sum is **6**. With `Option Strict On`, both lines are compile errors until you say what you mean, for example `5 \ 2` for integer division.

exercises.prompt:
What is the **second** line printed by this program?

```vb
Option Strict On

Module Program
    Sub Main()
        Console.WriteLine("1" & 2 & 3)
        Console.WriteLine(1 + 2 & 3)
    End Sub
End Module
```

feedback.message: Not yet — that is the first line. In the second, which operator binds more tightly, `+` or `&`?
Not yet — `&` always joins text; it never adds.

hints: Arithmetic operators have higher precedence than `&`.
So the second line computes `1 + 2` first.
exercises.solution: In the second line, `1 + 2` is evaluated first (arithmetic binds more tightly than concatenation), giving 3, and then `3 & 3` joins the text: `33`. The first line prints `123`.

exercises.prompt: Which of these lines are **compile errors** under `Option Strict On`? (Choose all that apply.)

options.label: `Dim n As Integer = "42"`
options.feedback: Yes. A string-to-integer conversion could fail, so it must be explicit (BC30512).

options.label: `Dim d As Double = 42`
options.feedback: Not yet — `Integer` to `Double` is a widening conversion that cannot lose information, so it is allowed.

options.label: `Dim o As Object = "x"` followed by `o.ToUpper()`
options.feedback: Yes. Calling a member on an `Object` is late binding, which Option Strict On forbids.

options.label: `Dim i As Integer = CInt(7.6)`
options.feedback: Not yet — `CInt` is an explicit conversion, so the compiler accepts it (it rounds to 8).

hints: Option Strict forbids implicit narrowing conversions and late binding.
Explicit conversions such as `CInt` are always allowed.
exercises.solution: (a) is an implicit narrowing conversion and (c) is late binding; both are compile errors under Option Strict On. (b) is a widening conversion and (d) is explicit, so both compile.

exercises.prompt: Which statements about Visual Basic today are accurate? (Choose all that apply.)

options.label: Visual Basic runs on current .NET (including .NET 10) for console apps, class libraries, Windows Forms and WPF
options.feedback: Yes. Microsoft supports these workloads on modern .NET.

options.label: Microsoft has said it does not plan to evolve Visual Basic as a language, and that its design is stable
options.feedback: Yes. The 2020 announcement and the current language strategy both say so.

options.label: Visual Basic 6 programs compile unchanged with the modern Visual Basic compiler
options.feedback: Not yet — VB.NET (2002) was not compatible with VB6; real VB6 programs need substantial rewriting.

options.label: VBA is the language used for macros in Microsoft Office
options.feedback: Yes. VBA is still part of Office and widely used for spreadsheet and database automation.

hints: Think about the 2020 announcement and the language strategy.
Was the move from VB6 to VB.NET a compatible upgrade?
exercises.solution: (a), (b) and (d) are accurate. (c) is not: Visual Basic .NET was a redesign on a new platform, and VB6 code must be rewritten (with tools to help) to run on .NET.

exercises.prompt: On a computer set to British regional settings (day/month/year), which date does the literal `#03/04/2026#` mean in Visual Basic?

options.label: 4 March 2026
options.feedback: Yes. Date literals always use month/day/year, whatever the regional settings.

options.label: 3 April 2026
options.feedback: Not yet — regional settings affect parsing and display of text, not date literals in code.

options.label: It depends on the computer's settings
options.feedback: Not yet — literals are fixed by the language, so code means the same thing everywhere.

options.label: It is a compile error because the day is ambiguous
options.feedback: Not yet — it is valid; the format is simply always month first.

hints: Literals in code cannot depend on the machine that compiles them.
exercises.solution: Visual Basic date literals are always month/day/year, so `#03/04/2026#` is 4 March 2026 on every computer. (Writing `#2026-03-04#` is also accepted and avoids the question entirely.) Parsing *text* with `Date.Parse`, by contrast, does use the current culture unless you pass one.
